title: What We Owe the Future
pitch: The case for longtermism: future people count, there could be a huge number of them, and we can shape their world, including by getting AI right.

chapters.g: Imagine living every human life in order. Most of that life is still in the future.
Future people matter, there could be vast numbers of them, and we can affect them.

chapters.t: You Can Shape the Course of History
chapters.g: Some moments are plastic, when choices can lock in for a long time.
The abolition of slavery as a case study in moral progress that was not inevitable.
How values could get locked in for a very long time, and how AI could make that much more likely.
Risks that could end humanity, including engineered pandemics and AI.
Could civilisation recover from a collapse, and what would we need?
The risk that technological progress stalls at a dangerous point.

chapters.t: Is It Good to Make Happy People?
chapters.g: Population ethics: is it good to bring more happy people into existence?
chapters.part: Part IV: Assessing the End of the World

chapters.t: Will the Future Be Good or Bad?
chapters.g: Reasons for and against expecting the future to be good.
chapters.part: Part IV: Assessing the End of the World

chapters.g: Practical steps: careers, donations, political action and personal choices.

ideas: Some choices today could lock in values for a very long time.
AI is one way values could get locked in.
Individuals can do a lot through careers and giving.

args.a: Positively influencing the long term future is a key moral priority.
args.c: Critics worry longtermism can justify ignoring present suffering or support risky reasoning about huge numbers.

questions: Do people a thousand years from now matter as much as people today?
How could AI lock in values, good or bad?

o: The view that positively influencing the long term future is a key priority

quiz.q: Which historical case does MacAskill use for moral change?
quiz.w: He argues abolition was not inevitable.
